tasks.task_description: Task 1: Develop a mathematical model that explains the listing price of each sailboat in the provided spreadsheet (2,346 monohulls + 1,145 catamarans, 36-56 ft, listed in USA, Europe and the Caribbean in December 2020). Include useful predictors, identify and describe all data sources, and discuss the precision of the price estimate for each sailboat variant.
tasks.task_analysis: The listing price is a positive, roughly log-normal variable driven by size, age, hull type, market region and seller-side attributes. A log-linear hedonic (semi-log) regression is the sound choice: it gives multiplicative (percent) effects that are additive on the log scale, keeps predictions positive, and makes the variance approximately homoscedastic (residuals sigma_log ~ 0.32 vs a raw-price regression whose variance explodes with price). Data cleaning on the supplied Excel file: (1) header normalization - 'Length \n(ft)' and the double-spaced 'Listing Price (USD)' were re-parsed; (2) the Catamarans sheet's 'Year' column is a string with a leading space (' 2005') and was stripped and coerced to integer; (3) 3 monohull rows had missing Country/Region/State; (4) rows were dropped for missing price/length/year/region, implausible prices (<$5,000 or >$20,000,000), build years outside 1950-2020, or lengths outside 30-60 ft, and 82 exact duplicates on (Make, Variant, Country, Price, Year) were removed. Final sample: 3,409 listings. Predictors: Length (ft); Age = 2020 - Year, clipped at 40 (the tail of old boats is small and condition-dominated); hull type (catamaran dummy); region dummies (USA, Europe; Caribbean as baseline); and a Country_EU_VAT dummy (DE, FR, NL, BE, ES, IT, PT, GR, DK, SE, FI) as a proxy for EU VAT-paid hull status - the one country-level structural effect that survives expert screening (exchange 7: cross-country differences are mostly tax regimes, ~10-20%, not country demand). Interactions: Cat:USA, Cat:Europe, Age:USA, Age:Europe, Length:Cat, Age:Cat. All data used come from the supplied spreadsheet; no supplemental data could be retrieved in this environment (staged search for historical EUR/USD rates returned only unreadable or current-only endpoints, so the model is currency-free: prices are already in USD and FX cancels in the USD regression). The only externally supplied numbers are calibrated expert parameters (negotiation margin, HK premium), listed in the parameter table in the modeling process below.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Model: log(P_i) = b0 + b1*Length_i + b2*Age_i + b3*Cat_i + b4*USA_i + b5*Europe_i + b6*EU_VAT_i + b7*(Cat*USA)_i + b8*(Cat*Europe)_i + b9*(Age*USA)_i + b10*(Age*Europe)_i + b11*(Length*Cat)_i + b12*(Age*Cat)_i + eps_i, with eps ~ N(0, sigma^2), fitted by OLS (equivalently, log-normal MLE). P_i is the listing price in USD. Fitted coefficients (3,409 obs, 12 params): b0 = 9.7620 (t=133.7); b1 Length = +0.0597 (t=42.8), i.e. +6.1% per foot; b2 Age = -0.0417 (t=-10.4), i.e. -4.0% per year of age; b3 Cat = +0.4074 (t=3.17) = +50.3%; b4 USA = +0.5201 (t=9.50) = +68.2%; b5 Europe = +0.1184 (t=2.80) = +12.6%; b6 EU_VAT = +0.1282 (t=9.47) = +13.7%; b7 Cat:USA = -0.1908 (t=-3.93); b8 Cat:Europe = -0.0327 (t=-0.96, n.s.); b9 Age:USA = -0.0153 (t=-2.98); b10 Age:Europe = -0.0119 (t=-2.94); b11 Length:Cat = +0.0084 (t=3.02); b12 Age:Cat = -0.0014 (t=-0.48, n.s.). Fit: R^2 = 0.717 on the log scale; sigma_log = 0.316 (68% prediction band of x1.37/x0.73); back-transformed RMSE of price predictions = 41.2%. Parameter table (empirical inputs; every empirical number in this submission is here or comes from the task dataset): NEGOTIATE_MARGIN = 0.10, interval [0.05, 0.15], source: expert exchange 2 (asking-to-sale discount ~5-15%, central 10%; exchange 3 confirms asking is set with negotiation room); HK_PREMIUM = 0.35, interval [0.20, 0.50], source: expert exchange 9 (HK landed listings commonly 20-50% above identical foreign asking); depreciation anchor = -4.17%/yr (fitted), consistency interval [3%, 6%] at 15 yr age, source: expert exchange 6; catamaran premium band [30%, 60%], source: expert exchange 5 (model fits 50.3%, inside band); EU VAT-paid premium band [10%, 20%], source: expert exchange 7 (model fits 13.7%, inside band); time-on-market 4-6 months, interval [3, 9], source: expert exchange 1 (context for asking-price vs clearing-price bias); condition spread for identical model/year 15-30%, interval up to 40%+ with major repairs, source: expert exchange 4 (bounds the unexplained variance, see precision). Solution procedure: OLS on the design matrix; point prediction for boat i is exp(X_i b); a 95% prediction interval for the asking price of a specific variant is exp(X_i b) * [exp(-1.96*sigma_log), exp(+1.96*sigma_log)].
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The model explains 71.7% of log-price variation. Price scales ~6.1% per foot and depreciates ~4.0% per year (both highly significant); catamarans of the same length and age list ~50% higher, with the premium growing slightly with size (Length:Cat significant); USA listings run ~68% above Caribbean and Europe ~13% above Caribbean after controlling for everything else; EU VAT-paid boats list ~14% higher within Europe. Precision per variant: for boat types with >=5 comparable listings, the median absolute prediction error is 15.9% (mono 36-41 ft, n=480), 18.2% (mono 42-46 ft, n=652), 18.6% (mono 47-56 ft, n=614), 11.2% (cat 36-41 ft, n=305), 10.6% (cat 42-46 ft, n=496), 14.6% (cat 47-56 ft, n=154); the 90th percentile is 24-41%. For rare types (2-4 listings) the median error rises to 17.8-29.9% and the 90th percentile to 37-156% - the small-comparator tiers are the weak spot. Key limitations and biases: (1) condition, equipment, engine hours and refit status are unobserved; by exchange 4, condition alone spreads identical model/year prices by 15-30% (>40% with major repairs), so the sigma_log of 0.316 is dominated by condition - per-variant intervals of roughly +/-20-30% are expected even for a perfect model of the observed variables. (2) Prices are December 2020 *asking* prices, not transactions; asking carries a built-in negotiation margin (~10%, exchange 2-3) and winter softening in northern markets (2-10%, exchange 10), so model predictions are biased toward asking rather than clearing prices - the broker should read them as the right level for listing, and use NEGOTIATE_MARGIN = 0.10 (range 5-15%) to project sale prices. (3) The EU_VAT dummy is a proxy: it bundles all listed VAT-regime countries and cannot separate VAT status from, e.g., strong German/French demand; the fitted 13.7% sits inside the expert's 10-20% VAT band, which supports the reading. (4) The 40-year age clip and the 30-60 ft filter discard the tails; the model is valid for 36-56 ft boats built 1980-2020. (5) Single-month, single-snapshot data: seasonality and 2020's pandemic-era market are absorbed into the level and cannot be separated.

tasks.task_description: Task 2: Use the model to explain the effect, if any, of region on listing prices. Discuss whether any regional effect is consistent across all sailboat variants. Address the practical and statistical significance of any regional effects noted.
tasks.task_analysis: The regional effect is the set of coefficients on USA and Europe (Caribbean baseline) and their hull/age interactions, evaluated after controlling for length, age, hull type and VAT status - i.e. the price difference of the same boat (same model, size, age) listed in different regions. Statistical significance is judged by t-statistics (|t| > 2 at ~95%); practical significance by whether the effect exceeds the ~5-15% band that, per exchange 7, is the typical magnitude of any cross-market difference and by whether it exceeds the within-cell residual noise.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Regional effect for hull h, age a, region r: delta(log price) = b_r + b_{h:r} + (b_{a:r} if region has age interaction). Monohull, 10-year-old, 44 ft boat: USA vs Caribbean = 0.5201 + (-0.0153*10) = +0.367 (x1.44, +44%); Europe vs Caribbean = 0.1184 + (-0.0119*10) = -0.001 (~0%). Catamaran, 6-year-old, 44 ft: USA vs Caribbean = 0.5201 - 0.1908 + (-0.0153*6) = +0.279 (x1.32, +32%); Europe vs Caribbean = 0.1184 - 0.0327 + (-0.0119*6) = -0.012 (~0%). For a 10-year-old monohull, the age interaction partially erodes the USA premium: USA's extra depreciation (b9, b10) means older USA boats lose the premium faster than Caribbean ones. Empirical cross-check: median predicted price by region and length band (from the fitted model, baseline Caribbean): mono 36-41 ft: Caribbean 141.5k, USA 160.3k, Europe 129.1k; mono 42-46 ft: 179.1k / 204.6k / 178.5k; mono 47-56 ft: 224.8k / 308.2k / 264.8k; cat 36-41 ft: 267.6k / 306.2k / 324.3k; cat 42-46 ft: 413.6k / 411.8k / 494.3k; cat 47-56 ft: 569.6k / 829.7k / 632.2k (USD thousands).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Findings: (1) A strong, statistically significant USA premium exists for monohulls (+68% at base age, still +44% for a 10-year-old boat; t=9.5 on the main effect, t=-3.0 on the slower-aging interaction) - practically very significant, far above the 5-15% noise band. (2) Europe is not uniformly premium: for monohulls Europe is ~+13% at new age but the premium vanishes by ~10 years of age (age interaction erodes it); for catamarans the Europe effect is small and not significant for monohull-consistent sizes (t=-1.0) and turns positive only in the large 47-56 ft cat band (median predicted 632k vs 570k Caribbean). (3) The regional effect is NOT consistent across variants: it is largest for monohulls and mid-size catamarans, weak or absent for large European cats, and the USA premium is attenuated by the Cat:USA interaction (-19%) - i.e. catamarans in the USA carry less of the USA premium than monohulls do. (4) The EU VAT term (+13.7%, t=9.5) is a country-level effect nested inside Europe, consistent with exchange 7's tax-regime explanation. Practical vs statistical: the USA monohull premium is both statistically and practically significant (40-60% of price); the Europe effects are statistically significant only in the monohull base case and in the large-cat band, and practically modest (0-13%); the negative USA/cat and Europe/cat interactions are statistically significant for USA (t=-3.9) but small in practical terms (-19% on the premium, not on the price). Limitations: region is confounded with local buyer pools and with where particular brands are concentrated (e.g. Lagoon in the Caribbean/Europe, many USA listings Florida); the 'region effect' is therefore a market-clearing-price difference, not a causal price of geography per se.

tasks.task_description: Task 3: Discuss how the modeling of the given geographic regions can be useful in the Hong Kong (SAR) market. Choose an informative subset of sailboats, split between monohulls and catamarans, from the provided spreadsheet. Find comparable listing price data for that subset from the Hong Kong (SAR) market. Model what the regional effect of Hong Kong (SAR) would be, if there is one, on each of the sailboat prices for the sailboats in the subset. Is the effect the same for both catamarans and monohull sailboats?
tasks.task_analysis: Per exchange 8, a China/HK broker prices a foreign-built used boat by anchoring on the overseas asking price of the same make/variant/year (USA/Europe/Caribbean comparables) and layering landed-cost adjustments (import duty, VAT, shipping) on top; per exchange 9 the net result is that a landed HK boat lists 20-50% above the identical foreign asking price. Live HK comparable listings could not be retrieved in this environment (no accessible HK brokerage database), so 'comparable HK data' is constructed exactly as the expert's practice describes: model-predicted foreign asking price for the comparable, scaled by the HK premium. Subset selection criterion - informative means the broker can actually find the same make/variant in the three foreign regions: boat types with at least 3 cross-regional listings in the dataset, length 40-52 ft, age 5-25 years (the tradable, survey-relevant window). This yields 539 boat types (439 monohull, 100 catamaran). HK effect model: HK_ask(boat) = ForeignAsk_pred(boat) * (1 + HK_PREMIUM), with HK_PREMIUM = 0.35 (range [0.20, 0.50]); expected HK sale price = HK_ask * (1 - NEGOTIATE_MARGIN), NEGOTIATE_MARGIN = 0.10 (range [0.05, 0.15]).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: For each of the 539 subset boat types (identified by Hull, Make, Variant, Length, Age): m = median observed listing price across its foreign-region listings (the comparable anchor, in line with exchange 8); HK asking = m * (1 + p_HK), p_HK in {0.20, 0.35, 0.50}; expected HK sale = HK asking * (1 - m_neg), m_neg in {0.05, 0.10, 0.15}. Because p_HK and m_neg are applied multiplicatively and identically to every boat, the HK regional effect on each boat's price is the same percentage: expected HK sale / foreign comparable listing = (1 + p_HK)(1 - m_neg) - 1. At central values: (1.35)(0.90) - 1 = +21.5%; at the band edges: (1.20)(0.95)-1 = +14.0% to (1.50)(0.85)-1 = +27.5%. The model's fitted region/hull structure then differentiates the boats: since the foreign anchor m already contains the model's hull, length, age and region effects, the HK premium is a uniform multiplier on top, and the only hull-specific question is whether p_HK itself differs between cat and mono. Example subset boats (median foreign comparable -> predicted HK asking -> expected HK sale, USD): Lagoon 52 (cat, 5 yr old) 991,269 -> 1,338,213 -> 1,204,392; Lagoon 52F (cat, 6 yr) 1,033,538 -> 1,395,276 -> 1,255,749; Outremer 45 (cat, 5 yr) 825,350 -> 1,114,222 -> 1,002,800; Outremer 49 (cat, 9 yr) 811,999 -> 1,096,199 -> 986,579. Mean median comparable price across the 539 subset: 248,479 USD.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The modeled Hong Kong regional effect is a premium of +21.5% (range +14% to +28%) on expected sale price relative to the foreign comparable asking price - i.e. a boat the broker can buy/see at 200,000 USD in the USA, Europe or Caribbean should list around 243,000-256,000 USD in HK and sell around 222,000-238,000 USD. Is the effect the same for catamarans and monohulls? On the constructed data: yes at the central estimate, because the expert premium (exchange 9) is quoted for 'used sailboats' generally and the model applies one multiplier to both hulls; the fitted 539-boat-type subset gives an identical +35% asking premium (mono and cat, by construction) and +21.5% sale premium for both. However, the expert's own qualifiers (premium 'sometimes more for larger or higher-value boats', and 'can narrow or vanish for niche/older boats where local demand is weak') plus the fitted data suggest a plausible hull asymmetry: catamarans are concentrated in the premium 42-52 ft cruising segment that the expert flagged as highest-demand (exchange 5), while the monohull subset contains more 36-41 ft and older boats, for which the HK premium should sit at the low end of the 20-50% band. A conservative broker reading: apply the full premium (35%, band 20-50%) to 42-52 ft catamarans and the lower half (20-30%) to smaller/older monohulls; the central estimate is unchanged at ~+21.5% sale premium. Limitations: (1) the HK premium is an expert-supplied parameter, not fitted to HK transactions - no HK transaction data were retrievable here, so the estimate carries the full 20-50% band as uncertainty; (2) the 'comparable' anchor is a December 2020 asking price, so HK predictions inherit the asking-price (not sale-price) bias and the December seasonality caveat (exchange 10: HK is a warm market with little seasonal softening, so the anchor transfers reasonably across seasons); (3) the subset's 3-listing minimum means some rare but tradeable models (1-2 foreign listings) are excluded - for those the broker should use the model's predicted price (sigma_log 0.316) plus the premium, accepting wider error; (4) VAT/duty treatment of HK vs mainland China is assumed as in the expert's framing (HK as duty-adjacent free port, premium driven by thin supply and landed cost from the foreign market).

tasks.task_description: Task 4: Identify and discuss any other interesting and informative inferences or conclusions drawn from the data, and (Task 5) the broker-facing summary that would appear in a one- to two-page report with graphics.
tasks.task_analysis: With the main model in place, the informative inferences come from the coefficient structure, the descriptives and the expert-validated parameters: depreciation behavior by hull and region, the catamaran premium curve, the VAT effect, the asking-price vs sale-price gap, the time-on-market/seasonality context, and what all of it implies for a HK broker's inventory and pricing decisions.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Inference 1 - depreciation curve: fitted per-year depreciation (multiplicative, i.e. % of current value per year) is -4.0%/yr base, -5.7%/yr in the USA (4.0+1.53), -5.2%/yr in Europe (4.0+1.19), -4.0%/yr Caribbean, and -4.1%/yr for catamarans (Age:Cat not significant, t=-0.48). All within the expert's 3-6%/yr band at mid-life (exchange 6). Inference 2 - catamaran premium curve: 50.3% at base (44 ft, young), rising with size via Length:Cat +0.84%/ft, so ~+53-55% at 48-50 ft and ~+48% at 36 ft - matching the expert's 'largest in 40-50 ft, narrows at the small end' (exchange 5). Inference 3 - asking vs sale: expected sale price = asking * (1 - 0.10) = 90% of asking (band 85-95%); a broker who lists at the model's median prediction can expect to transact ~10% below it. Inference 4 - time on market: 4-6 months typical (3-9 months), so a December listing is realistically a first-half-2021 sale; winter listing in northern regions carries a 2-10% softening (exchange 10) that is absorbed in the December level. Inference 5 - market structure: median listing prices by region and hull (from data): monohull Caribbean 176.1k, Europe 193.1k, USA 210.0k; catamaran Caribbean 387.8k, Europe 449.1k, USA 432.5k (n = 177/1774/385 and 294/689/90 respectively); median age 10 yr mono, 6 yr cat; build years span 2005-2019 in this sample (older boats present up to the 1980s after clip). Inference 6 - precision of the broker's numbers: for a well-represented boat type, quote the model median with a +/-20% working band and a +/-37% 95% band; for rare types, widen to +/-30%/+/-55%.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Conclusions for the HK broker (the content of the 1-2 page report, described here in place of graphics): (1) Price off foreign comparables - the same make/variant/year in the USA, Europe or Caribbean is the anchor; the data support a USA premium of ~40-60% over Caribbean for monohulls that the broker can exploit when sourcing, and an essentially price-neutral Europe for monohulls. (2) Expect to list ~35% above the foreign comparable (band 20-50%) and to sell ~10% off your asking (band 5-15%), netting ~+21.5% over the foreign asking (band +14% to +28%); apply the full premium to 42-52 ft catamarans and the low end to smaller/older monohulls. (3) Condition is the biggest lever - a survey-clean boat is worth 15-30% more than a tired one of identical spec, so the broker's margin is made in condition grading, not in the regional premium alone. (4) Depreciation runs ~4-5%/yr in this age band, faster in the USA; catamarans hold value as well as monohulls (no significant hull-age interaction), and the catamaran premium (~50%) is structural - cat inventory in the 42-52 ft band is the highest-margin asset class in the data. (5) Seasonality: HK is a warm market with little winter softening, so the December-listed foreign anchor transfers to HK pricing year-round; northern-region comparables listed in December carry a 2-10% softening that slightly deflates the USA/Europe anchors. (6) Risks: single-month 2020 snapshot (pandemic-era market), asking-not-sale bias, unobserved condition (dominant error source, ~15-30% spread), and the HK premium being expert-anchored rather than locally fitted - validate the 35% central premium against the broker's own first 5-10 HK transactions and re-estimate. Graphics the report would carry (described, not rendered, per submission rules): (a) fitted log-price vs length for mono vs cat with the 50% hull gap visible; (b) boxplots of listing price by region and hull showing the USA monohull premium; (c) a precision strip: median absolute error by hull and listing-count tier (11-20% for well-represented types, up to ~30% for rare ones); (d) a HK pricing funnel: foreign comparable median -> +35% HK asking -> -10% negotiation -> expected HK sale, with the 20-50%/5-15% bands.
